According to a report yesterday, Apple had considered launching a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but ultimately decided to abandon the plan.

Bloomberg points out three reasons behind this decision, one of which is the desire not to conflict with the stance Steve Jobs held when he launched the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the decisive factor…

A short Apple Pencil designed for use with the iPhone Ultra does sound like an appealing concept on the surface. The device is essentially an iPhone that can transform into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities is obviously a reasonable approach.

When Samsung launched the Galaxy Note phone-tablet hybrid back in 2011, it came with an S-Pen stylus. The idea at the time was to position the device as a tool that could partially replace paper notebooks. It developed over ten years and built a loyal following before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman lists three reasons why Apple ultimately shelved the idea:

  • Having a Pencil attached to the side of the device would feel clumsy when holding it, rather than being fixed at the top
  • It would conflict with Steve's view that a stylus is an inferior substitute for the finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't think the first reason would be the main consideration, since securing the stylus at the top of the device would have been a perfectly viable option. Although this would require an extremely short design, I think it could still work reasonably well.

I also disagree with the second reason. What Steve objected to back then was not the idea of a smartphone being usable with a stylus, but the notion that every model would have to rely on one. The real breakthrough was making the iPhone genuinely designed to be operated with the finger.

In any case, Steve was also famously against adding a touchscreen to the Mac on ergonomic grounds, yet we are still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro models to include a touchscreen, showing that Apple is not afraid to overturn positions its co-founder once held.

I think the third factor is the real reason the idea was stillborn. The surface of a folding display is inevitably far thinner and more pliable than the screens on existing devices. Reports indicate that Apple waited a very long time before launching its first foldable iPhone precisely because of concerns about the display's appearance and durability, and adding an Apple Pencil repeatedly scraping across it would only cause damage to both.

If Apple could solve this problem in the future, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
